title: sie (they) — They
description: Practise changing the object with sie (they): present, future and past.
intro: Every example uses Sie as its subject, meaning they in this file. Sie here is plural they: sie sehen, sie geben, sie werden, sie haben. It is capitalized only because it begins the sentence. Use sich when the subject is also the object or recipient. Object sie/ihnen refer to another group here; sich has the reciprocal reading each other. Keep the subject fixed and vary whom the subject sees or to whom the subject gives the book. Sehen takes an accusative object. Geben takes a dative recipient plus das Buch as the accusative thing. The highlighted key is the object or recipient. English labels: (s) singular, (p) plural, (f) formal.

sections.title: sie (they) — changing the object
sections.explanation: Start with the present-tense accusative and dative lists, then compare the same object choices in Futur I and Perfekt. Short sentences omit final full stops.
sections.rule: Sie sehen + Akkusativ | Sie geben + Dativ + das Buch

entries.explanation: The subject and verb stay fixed. Change the accusative object.

examples.note: Singular feminine: her.
Plural: them. Same German spelling as her; context distinguishes the meaning. A different group from the subject; use sich for each other/themselves.
Formal object or recipient: always capitalized; one or more addressees.
Reciprocal reading: each other. A reflexive ourselves/yourselves/themselves reading is also possible in context.

entries.explanation: The subject, verb and das Buch stay fixed. Change only the dative recipient. Ihm is translated as him here, but can also refer to a neuter noun.

examples.note: Masculine or neuter dative; translated him here.
A different group from the subject; use sich for each other/themselves.
Formal object or recipient: always capitalized; one or more addressees.

examples.english: They give each other the book
examples.note: Reciprocal reading: each other. A reflexive ourselves/yourselves/themselves reading is also possible in context.

entries.explanation: Use werden plus sehen to practise the future tense. The infinitive goes at the end and the object's case stays the same. German also uses the present tense with a future time expression.

examples.note: Singular feminine: her.

Formal object or recipient: always capitalized; one or more addressees.

entries.explanation: Use werden plus geben to practise the future tense. The infinitive goes at the end and the object's case stays the same. German also uses the present tense with a future time expression.
entries.pattern: Sie werden + Dativ + das Buch + geben

entries.explanation: Use haben plus gesehen for a past event. Perfekt is common in conversation. The English examples use saw; depending on context, have/has seen is also possible. The object's case stays the same.
